title: Very many Reformed side with the Thomists: efficacious premotion to every act, good and evil
source_text: XL. Plurimi tamen inter Theologos Reformatos censent cum Thomae Schola, Deum non solum ad singulos creaturarum actus simul cum iis concurrere atque cooperari, sed etiam creaturas nihil agere posse, nisi ad hos & illos actus efficaciter a Deo praemoveantur & praedeterminentur: idque locum habere tam in causis liberis quam in necessariis, & tam in malis actibus quam in bonis; licet Deus non moveat, neque praedeterminet ad malitiam & pravitatem actus, sed tantum ad illud quod est in eo positivum & naturaliter bonum. Ac quemadmodum ex eorum sententia causa secunda sine tali praedeterminatione nihil agere & operari potest, ita quoque illa supposita, impossibile est eam non agere atque operari.
pass_a_gloss: Yet very many among the Reformed Theologians think with the School of Thomas, that God not only concurs and cooperates with each of the acts of creatures together with them, but also that creatures can do nothing, unless they are efficaciously premoved and predetermined by God to these and those acts: and that this has place as well in free causes as in necessary, and as well in evil acts as in good; although God does not move, nor predetermine to the malice and depravity of the act, but only to that which is in it positive and naturally good. And as according to their opinion the second cause without such predetermination can act and operate nothing, so also that being supposed, it is impossible that it should not act and operate.
pass_b_english: Very many Reformed theologians, however, side with the school of Thomas. They hold that God not only concurs and cooperates with creatures in each of their acts, but that creatures can do nothing unless God efficaciously premoves and predetermines them to this act or that.

This holds, they say, for free causes as much as for necessary ones, and for evil acts as much as for good ones, although God does not move or predetermine to the malice and depravity of the act, only to what is positive and naturally good in it. And just as on their view the secondary cause can do or perform nothing without such predetermination, so too, once it is given, the cause cannot fail to act and perform.

choices.why: Kept as the Thomist technical term; Le Blanc explains 'physical' as opposed to 'moral', not to 'supernatural'.
